request.system:
You classify one recorded call at Aegis Cloud Security, a B2B SaaS company, against a fixed theme taxonomy (version v1).

You receive the full transcript as numbered turns in the form "[index] Speaker (side): sentence". side is "customer" (works at an outside company) or "aegis_staff" (works at Aegis). You are given nothing else about the call: no title, no call type, no summary. Judge only from the words in the transcript.

THEMES (what kind of conversation it is; pick by what the call is mostly about):
1. Commercial Renewals and Retention: Renewals, contracts, pricing and SLA negotiation, churn risk, expansion deals. Boundary: If a call is mainly about product adoption with renewal as an aside, use Product Adoption, Feedback and Expansion.
2. Product Adoption, Feedback and Expansion: Previews, launches, early access, roadmap input, feature requests, adoption and compliance-readiness reviews of the product, and internal launch-readiness reviews. Boundary: The module belongs in the product area field, not in the theme. Renewal talk that is only an aside stays here.
3. Incident and Outage Response: War rooms, root cause, remediation plans, customer impact assessment, incident communication, postmortems, reliability reviews. Boundary: A single customer's technical fault that is not a platform incident belongs in Technical Integration and Performance Issues.
4. Technical Integration and Performance Issues: Support-style troubleshooting: SSO, SAML, SCIM, LDAP, MFA failures, connectors and SIEM integration, backup windows and throughput, report defects, API errors, internal scalability concerns. Boundary: Module-specific problems go here with the module in the product area field. A platform-wide outage is Incident and Outage Response.
5. Onboarding and Implementation Scoping: Kickoffs, deployment planning, architecture scoping, setup workshops. Boundary: Troubleshooting of an already deployed integration is Technical Integration and Performance Issues.
6. Billing and Usage Disputes: Invoices, overages, seat counts, billing adjustments. Boundary: Small theme (about 4 calls in the pilot); kept because it is distinct and actionable.
7. Competitive Strategy and Win/Loss: Competitive intelligence, battlecards, win/loss analysis, and customer-facing calls where the customer is evaluating alternatives. Boundary: Definition widened from the pilot's internal-only version to include customer calls about evaluating alternatives.
8. Internal Planning and Delivery Cadence: Standups, sprint planning, retros, all-hands, design and roadmap syncs with no customer or incident focus. Boundary: If a meeting is mainly an incident, use Incident and Outage Response.

Other / new theme: use only if no theme above fits. Then describe the call in one sentence in other_description. Other / new theme only if no theme fits. More than 10% of calls in Other triggers a taxonomy revision (new version, full re-run).

PRODUCT AREA (which module the call is about; exactly one):
- Detect: Threat detection, event ingestion, alerting.
- Comply: Compliance reporting and evidence mapping (including Comply v2).
- Protect: Backup, snapshots, disaster recovery (includes backup).
- Identity: Directory sync, SSO, SAML, SCIM, MFA, IAM governance.
- Platform/General: No single product dominates, or the call is cross-product.

INCIDENT: Set incident to '2026-03-detect-outage' (otherwise null) when the call's main purpose, or a major part of it, is the March 2026 Detect event-processing pipeline outage: cause, impact, remediation, customer communication or aftermath. A separate field so the outage story is visible across support, external and internal calls.

Return one record with:
- primary_theme: exactly one theme name copied from the list above, or "Other / new theme".
- tags: zero, one or two further theme names from the list that also clearly come up. Never repeat the primary theme. Empty when primary_theme is "Other / new theme".
- product_area: exactly one product area name copied from the list.
- incident: "2026-03-detect-outage" or null.
- other_description: one sentence if primary_theme is "Other / new theme", otherwise an empty string.
- evidence_quote: a short passage of at most 30 words that best supports primary_theme, copied EXACTLY, character for character, from the sentence part of ONE turn. Copy only the words after "Speaker (side): ". Never include the index, the speaker name, the side or the colon prefix. Do not paraphrase, do not shorten with "...", do not join text from different turns.
- confidence: "high" if clearly about the primary theme, "medium" if two themes compete, "low" if it fits poorly.
- taxonomy_version: "v1".

Return only JSON matching the schema.

[8] Kevin O'Brien (aegis_staff): That's correct. Six hours, approximately. And I — yeah, there's no softening that. That's a significant window.

[10] Kevin O'Brien (aegis_staff): Yeah, absolutely. So we've already implemented redundant processing nodes — so there's no longer a single point of failure in that ingestion layer. [12] Maria Santos (aegis_staff): That's a fair point, Charles.
[13] Charles Ng (customer): Two hours before we got any notification. My team was the one who flagged it to your support desk. We noticed our dashboards had gone stale before Aegis even sent us an alert. That's — I mean, that's backwards. A threat monitoring product should be monitoring itself.
[14] Kevin O'Brien (aegis_staff): You're absolutely right, and that's — honestly, that's the part that stings the most from our side too. The alerting on the internal failure was not working the way it should have. That's a gap we've identified and it's being addressed alongside the pipeline fix.
[15] Maria Santos (aegis_staff): Charles, can I ask — and I want to understand the full picture here — what was the actual impact on Helix during that window? Did anything slip through, or was it more of an exposure risk that you had to manage?
[16] Charles Ng (customer): Fortunately — and I say fortunately with a lot of emphasis there — nothing slipped through that we've found. But we spent, I don't know, twelve, fifteen person-hours doing a manual review of logs after the fact just to confirm that. My team basically had to do Aegis Detect's job manually for six hours and then audit it afterward. That's not a small thing for us.
[17] Maria Santos (aegis_staff): Yeah, that's — yeah. That's a real cost and I don't want to minimize it.
[18] Charles Ng (customer): And look, I like you guys. I've always liked working with your team. But I have to be transparent — this isn't happening in a vacuum. We've been having internal conversations about our security stack, and, um, we've been talking to VaultEdge as part of a broader vendor review. I'm not saying that to be threatening, I just — you should know where we're at.
[19] Maria Santos (aegis_staff): I appreciate you telling us that, Charles. I really do. Can you tell us a bit more about what's driving that review — is it primarily this incident, or were there concerns before?
[20] Charles Ng (customer): Honestly? It's both. This incident accelerated the conversation, but we've had some lower-level grumbles for a while. The alert noise from Detect has been higher than we'd like — a lot of false positives that my team has to triage. And the custom rule configuration, it's... it's more cumbersome than it should be for a platform at this price point.
[21] Kevin O'Brien (aegis_staff): The false positive rate — is that something you've flagged with support previously, or has it mostly been absorbed internally?
[22] Charles Ng (customer): Mostly absorbed internally, which I'll admit is partly on us for not escalating sooner. But there's also an expectation that a product this mature should have better out-of-the-box tuning, you know?
[23] Maria Santos (aegis_staff): Yeah, that's fair feedback and I want to make sure we capture that properly. On the rule configuration side — Kevin, is that something we can get eyes on specifically for Helix's environment?
[24] Kevin O'Brien (aegis_staff): Absolutely. Charles, I'd actually like to set up a separate working session just on the detection tuning — look at what rules you have configured, where the noise is coming from, and get you to a better baseline. That's something we can do in the next week or two.
[25] Charles Ng (customer): I mean, I'm open to that. I just want to make sure it's not a band-aid. Like, if the underlying product has structural issues, tuning sessions aren't going to change my view on the platform.
[26] Maria Santos (aegis_staff): That's completely reasonable and I hear you. I don't want to oversell a tuning session either. What I'd want to understand better is — when you're talking to VaultEdge, what is it that they're showing you that's resonating? Because I want to understand if there are genuine capability gaps on our side.
[27] Charles Ng (customer): Uh, well — their detection pipeline architecture, from what they've shown us, is distributed by design. Which, in light of what just happened, is obviously appealing. They've also been talking about their alert correlation engine, which is supposedly a lot better at suppressing redundant alerts. We haven't done a full POC yet so I can't say for sure how it actually performs.
[28] Kevin O'Brien (aegis_staff): Okay, that's helpful. And just so you know — the redundant node architecture we've now deployed is functionally similar to what a distributed-by-design approach would give you. I want to make sure you're evaluating the current state, not where we were a week ago.
[29] Maria Santos (aegis_staff): Kevin, can you — would it make sense to put together something in writing that documents the architecture changes? Like a proper technical brief that Charles can share with his leadership?
[30] Kevin O'Brien (aegis_staff): Yeah, I can do that. I can have a technical summary of the remediation and the new architecture ready by end of this week.
[31] Charles Ng (customer): That would actually be useful. My CTO is asking questions and right now I'm the one translating the situation upward, so having something formal would help.
[32] Kevin O'Brien (aegis_staff): Totally, and I'll make it CTO-readable — high level but technically substantive, not just marketing language.
[33] Maria Santos (aegis_staff): Charles, I also want to put something on the table — and I want to be thoughtful about how I say this because I don't want it to feel transactional. But given the impact this caused, I want to talk about what we can do to make this right beyond just the technical fix. I'd like to bring a proposal to you by end of week.
[34] Charles Ng (customer): I appreciate that, Maria. I'll be honest, though — it's going to take more than a service credit to rebuild my confidence here. I need to see that this kind of failure mode is genuinely off the table going forward.
[35] Maria Santos (aegis_staff): Understood. And I think the combination of the architecture brief from Kevin, the tuning session, and whatever we put together commercially — I want all of that to come together as a package, not just a check in a box. Can we plan to reconnect next week to go through it together?
[36] Charles Ng (customer): Yeah, next week works. I'd say mid-week — Tuesday or Wednesday. And I'd want my security lead, Priya, on that call as well.
[37] Maria Santos (aegis_staff): Perfect, we'll get that scheduled. And Charles — again, I'm sorry. This shouldn't have happened and I want to make sure that when we talk next week, you feel like we've actually addressed the things you've raised today, not just acknowledged them.
[38] Charles Ng (customer): I hear you. I'll see how next week looks. Thanks for getting on the call today, both of you.
[39] Kevin O'Brien (aegis_staff): Thanks Charles, talk soon.
